I farm in Quzhou County, so I will keep to the cropping pattern I trust most for this area: winter wheat followed by summer maize. At my age, I want something steady, familiar, and manageable with the labor I can handle. I would not spread myself across too many crops, because that adds risk and makes field work harder. Wheat and maize fit the local climate, the irrigation conditions, and the machinery I am most likely to use.

For the winter season, I will plant winter wheat on all my land. I would use improved seed, not old saved seed, because I want more stable emergence, better disease resistance, and more reliable yield. I would prepare the land with rotary tillage because it is easier for me than deep ploughing every year and still gives a decent seedbed. I would apply a moderate amount of nitrogen, with phosphorus and potassium as base fertilizer, then irrigate a few key times, especially around overwintering recovery, jointing, and grain filling if water is available. I would not spray too many times, only enough to control the main diseases, weeds, and aphids when needed.

After wheat harvest, I will plant summer maize right away. I would also use improved or hybrid maize seed because maize responds well to better seed and gives me more dependable production. I would keep fertilizer fairly balanced, but maize would get a little more nitrogen because it needs strong growth after sowing and before tasseling. I would reduce tillage pressure after wheat and use rotary tillage again so I can turn the crop around quickly. Irrigation for maize would be limited to the most important periods, because summer rain helps, but I would still water if the field turns dry around jointing or silking. I would keep pesticide use limited and practical, focusing on weeds early and then insects or disease only if pressure becomes obvious.
